doc_description: This document provides a comprehensive overview of Dr. Abdeen Khairy's life and heroic contributions as the first doctor to sacrifice himself during the 1976 Ebola epidemic, detailing his biography, medical career, and the circumstances surrounding his tragic illness and death.

structure.title: Historical Perspectives
structure.summary: The partial document discusses the life and contributions of Dr. Abdeen Khairy, who is recognized as the first doctor to sacrifice his life in the fight against the Ebola epidemic in 1976. It provides a brief biography of Dr. Khairy, detailing his early life, education, and medical career, including his schooling in Northern Province, secondary education in Port Sudan, and medical training at the University of Khartoum. The document also mentions his roles as a medical officer in various hospitals, including Omdurman Teaching Hospital and Maridi Hospital in what is now South Sudan.

nodes.summary: The partial document discusses the life and contributions of Dr. Abdeen Khairy, who is recognized as the first doctor to sacrifice his life in the fight against the Ebola epidemic in 1976. It provides a biographical overview of Dr. Khairy, detailing his early life, education, and medical career in Sudan, including his work in various hospitals. The document highlights the circumstances under which he contracted the Ebola virus while serving in Maridi District Hospital, where he was the only doctor present during a severe outbreak that resulted in the deaths of many hospital staff. It also includes accounts from Dr. Abdelrahman Ali, a colleague who assisted in transporting Dr. Khairy to Juba for medical attention, and emphasizes the urgency and fear surrounding the outbreak. Additionally, the document features maps and a table summarizing the biographies of other individuals involved in the narrative.

http://www.sudanjp.orgDr. Abdeen Khairy contracted the Ebola 
virus disease while doing his “Hardship 
Area Duty” in Maridi District Hospital 
in Equatoria Province, Sudan (currently, 
South Sudan) [Figures 2A, 2B and 2C]. 
He was the only doctor there when 
alarming numbers of hospital staff 
were infected, and 41 staff members 
died [2]. This instilled fear and panic 
into the Medical Staff who began not 
to come to Hospital for work except 
for few brave ones, among whom some died.  He was escorted from Maridi to 
Juba by his colleague Dr. Abdelrahman 
Ali (Medical Officer in Lewi District 
Hospital near Mardidi, [Figure 2D]).  
On interviewing Dr. Abdelrahman, who 
was born in 1949 in Al Sair (one of 
Argo Island villages)[ Table 1, Figure 
3A], he said in September 1976 he was 
doing his Hardship Area Duty in Lewi 
District Hospital about 65 miles from 
Maridi. The Military Commander in Miridi contacted him, telling him that 
Dr. Abdeen Khairy is very sick in Maridi 
Hospital and he is bringing him to Lewi 
by a military vehicle. They reached Lewi 
late in the evening and they continued 
without delay to Juba (Figure 2B), 
reaching it next day morning. Dr. Abdeen 
was left in the Doctor’s Rest House and 
Dr. Abdelrahman met Dr. Justin Yak the 
Regional Minister of Health who gave 
him 5 return tickets to Khartoum, so that an investigating team (physicians, 
virologist and microbiologist) can come 
to Juba, as he did not want Dr. Abdeen 
to go to Khartoum with the possibility of 
spreading this haemorrhagic fever, with 
significantly high mortality, to the North.Figure 1 – Maps 
showing (signs): (A) 
Delgo, (B) Port Sudan 
and (C) Kosti, Sudan.
(Based on Google™ 
Earth map).

Dr Hisham Aman:
• Born in 1947 in Burri, Khartoum, Sudan
• Elementary School : Khartoum
• Secondary School : Khartoum
• University  : Faculty of Medicine, University of Khartoum, Sudan [1]
• Currently   : Consultant Physician, Saudi Arabia

The narrative highlights the urgency of the situation, the discussions with health officials, and the eventual decision to transport Dr. Abdeen back to Khartoum for better care. The document includes maps and figures to provide geographical context and visual references related to the events described.

http://www.sudanjp.orgIn the same day after arriving in Khartoum, Dr. 
Abdelrahman met with the Undersecretary of the 
Ministry of Health (Dr. Abbas Mokhtar)[3]. They 
tried to contact different physicians in the field of 
tropical medicine but they failed since this was during 
Eid al-Fitr Holiday (1396 Hijri Calendar). Lastly, they 
decided to go to Dr. Abdulgaffar Abdulraheem [3], 
Director of the Tropical Diseases Hospital, Omdurman 
(1976-1986) in his house (Figure 4). Dr. Abdulgaffar 
decided to fly next day to Juba accompanied by 
Dr. Abdelrahman. When they reached Juba, Dr. 
Abdulgaffar asked the pilot not to leave Juba without his notice since he might be accompanied by a doctor who is seriously ill. He immediately went to see Dr. 
Abdeen, and found him extremely ill. He met Dr. 
Justin Yak, the Regional Minister of Health, and a 
lengthy discussion was held as Dr. Justin was insisting 
not to move Dr. Abdeen since the disease may spread 
in the North. But Dr. Abdulgaffar told him that Dr. 
Abdeen was moribund and it was better for him to 
die besides his family.  So Dr. Abdulgaffaar, accepting 
to take full responsibility, flew back with Dr. Abdeen 
in the same plane to Khartoum. Dr. Abdelrahman Ali 
went back to his station in Lewi.

nodes.summary: The partial document discusses a medical case involving Dr. Abdeen Khairi, who was critically ill with a suspected hemorrhagic fever upon his arrival in Khartoum in September 1976. It details the efforts of Dr. Abdelrahman and Dr. Abdulgaffar Abdulraheem to secure medical assistance for Dr. Abdeen, including a visit to the Tropical Diseases Hospital and a flight back to Khartoum despite concerns about disease transmission. The narrative describes Dr. Abdeen's deteriorating condition, his symptoms, and the lack of a definitive diagnosis or specific treatment during his hospital stay. The document also mentions the emotional impact of his illness on family members and medical staff, culminating in his eventual death. Additionally, it includes references to medical archives and notable figures in Sudanese medicine.

On the day of his arrival (September 1976), I was the 
Medical House Officer on call at Dr. Abdulmoniem 
Wasfi’s Unit; the Registrar was Dr. Hisham Aman. Dr. 
Khairy was brought by ambulance from Khartoum 
Airport to the Medical Casualty, and I was among the 
team (nurses and the ambulance driver) who moved 
him to stretcher into the Casualty. He was examined 
by me and I endorsed him to Dr. Aman, the Registrar 
who made the arrangements for admission to the South 
Block section of Khartoum Teaching Hospital.  He 
was conscious, but febrile and having some epistaxis.  
There was a lot of crowd outside the Casualty.  But most of the people were scared.  After his arrival, a lot 
of investigations were done and we were not aware of 
the disease but admitted him as haemorrhagic fever 
for investigations. As no definite diagnosis was made, no specific treatment was given. During his short stay in the hospital, his condition deteriorated despite the 
supportive treatment he was receiving.  
He was visited by the late Mr. Ahmed Abdulaziz, 
the Hospital Director [6,7].  He was attended by his 
nephew Najmeldin Mohamed Nour. Najmeldeen is 
the son of Dr. Abdeen’s sister. On his interview, he 
said after the arrival of Dr. Abdeen from Juba, he was 
attending with him from day one. Initially he was 
fully conscious and having bleeding from the nose 
with continuous fever for days. He started to bleed from different sites with bloody vomitus and stools 
and started to ask about people who died long time 
ago and was not aware of his surroundings and telling 
me that I have not seen you for many days. Then, he 
went in coma and after a day or two, he died.

nodes.title: REFERENCE
nodes.summary: The partial document recounts the medical case of Dr. Khairy, who was admitted to Khartoum Teaching Hospital in September 1976 after arriving from Khartoum Airport. The author, a Medical House Officer, describes the initial examination and the circumstances surrounding Dr. Khairy's condition, which included fever and epistaxis. Despite being conscious upon arrival, his health deteriorated rapidly, leading to multiple organ bleeding and eventual coma. The document highlights the lack of a definitive diagnosis, resulting in no specific treatment being administered. It also mentions the involvement of hospital staff, including the Hospital Director and Dr. Khairy's nephew, who provided support during his illness. The document concludes with references to various medical sources and archives related to the case and the broader context of viral hemorrhagic fever.
